questions.question: Explain why WHAT a country trades matters more for development than HOW MUCH it trades, using South Africa's trade profile and the terms of trade mechanism.
questions.expected_answer: The decisive distinction is between primary products — raw ores, crops, timber — and manufactured goods, which carry skill and technology folded in. Most value is added during processing, so a country exporting raw materials and importing machinery sells cheap and buys expensive: the peripheral trade profile. Commodities are priced on world markets where no single producer controls the ruling price, and those prices lurch — a frost in Brazil sends coffee soaring, a Chinese construction slump drags iron ore and platinum down — so commodity-dependent economies like oil-driven Angola ride a rollercoaster they do not steer. The terms of trade mechanism deepens the problem: because raw materials face endless competition and substitution while manufactured goods shelter behind patents and brands, primary prices slide against manufactured prices over the long run, so primary exporters must ship ever more tonnage to afford the same machine — running up a downward escalator. Exporting more raw material therefore rarely closes the gap; changing the basket does. South Africa illustrates both sides: platinum, gold, coal and iron ore exports carry the commodity risk, while the vehicles assembled in Kariega, East London, Durban and Rosslyn are value-added exports — exactly the basket policy tries to grow.

questions.question: Evaluate the impact of globalisation on developing countries, giving at least two gains and two costs with South African examples.
questions.expected_answer: Globalisation — the deepening interconnection of economies driven by container shipping, instant communication and lowered trade barriers, with the transnational corporation as its signature institution — pulls in both directions. Gains: whole-world markets instead of neighbours only; investment, factories and technology flowing into developing economies; hundreds of millions of manufacturing jobs, lifting East Asia from poverty at historic speed; and cheaper goods for consumers. South African examples include vehicle plants wired into global supply chains, citrus and wine on northern shelves, and Shoprite and MTN trading across the continent. Costs: benefits cluster in a few favoured locations, reproducing the core-periphery pattern; TNCs out-bargain small governments, extracting tax holidays, repatriating profits and threatening relocation — the race to the bottom; infant industries can be flattened before maturing, as when South African clothing and textile factories, including Newcastle's, shed tens of thousands of jobs to cheaper Asian imports; and interconnection transmits shocks, with the 2008 Wall Street crisis cutting South African exports and jobs within months. Balanced verdict: a powerful engine that pulls unevenly — those with skills, infrastructure and bargaining power ride it, while those without can be run over.

questions.question: Describe the export-led development strategy as the Asian Tigers ran it, and critically examine whether South Africa can repeat it.
questions.expected_answer: The strategy grows an economy by selling manufactured exports to the world market: begin with cheap-labour manufactures such as textiles, bank the foreign exchange, reinvest deliberately in education and infrastructure, and climb the value ladder — textiles to steel to ships to cars to semiconductors. South Korea ran this from an income level among the world's poorest in 1960 to developed status within two generations, with an active state that sheltered infant industries, steered credit and made support conditional on export success; China later ran the same play at continental scale. The critical limits: the strategy presumes open, growing markets, which flood if everyone climbs at once; the Tigers enjoyed unrepeatable access and geopolitical backing; the bottom rungs were carried by low wages, long hours and suppressed unions, raising the question of who pays for take-off; export economies import shocks, as 2008 showed; and the environmental bill was deferred into East Asia's smog. South Africa runs export-led elements — vehicles under motor industry programmes, citrus and wine, AGOA access — but climbs with burdens the Tigers never carried: distance from major markets, unreliable electricity, skills shortages and rigid input costs. Conclusion: a proven route, not a guaranteed one — it demands state capacity, education and dependable infrastructure, which are developmental achievements in themselves.
